uncited: Computes a representative camera pose (origin and orientation) from a set of input camera poses, typically used to initialize a scene or define a central viewing direction for volume rendering and NeRF training.

It differs from [Camera Pose Transformation](1672-camera-pose-transformation.md) by aggregating multiple poses into one, and from [Orbit Camera Basis Computation](1749-orbit-camera-basis-computation.md) by not assuming a fixed orbital path.
It addresses the problem of defining a canonical coordinate frame or initial camera position when no single pose is dominant.
The method computes an average translation and an average rotation.
Two primary approaches exist: a simple arithmetic mean (often used in early NeRF implementations) and an SVD-based orthogonalization (used in more robust pipelines).
Each pose is a $3 \times 4$ or $4 \times 4$ matrix representing the camera-to-world (c2w) transformation.
The first three columns are the rotation basis vectors (right, up, forward/view), and the fourth column is the translation (origin).
This method averages the translation vectors and the rotation basis vectors directly.
It is simple but does not guarantee the resulting rotation matrix is orthogonal.
**Compute Average Translation**: Calculate the mean of the translation columns (column index 3) across all poses.
**Compute Average Viewing Direction**: Sum the viewing direction vectors (typically column index 2, representing the negative z-axis in camera space) and normalize.
**Compute Average Up Vector**: Sum the up vectors (typically column index 1) and normalize.
**Construct Basis**: Compute the right vector (column 0) as the cross product of the up vector and the viewing direction to ensure orthogonality.
**Assemble Pose**: Construct the $3 \times 4$ matrix using `vec0`, `vec1`, `vec2`, and `center`.
This method averages the rotation matrices and uses Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to project the result onto the Special Orthogonal group $SO(3)$, ensuring a valid rotation matrix.
**Compute Mean Rotation Matrix**: Calculate the element-wise mean of the $3 \times 3$ rotation submatrices (columns 0-2).
**SVD Decomposition**: Perform SVD on `mean_rot`.
**Assemble Pose**: Concatenate `avg_rot` and `center` (reshaped to a column vector) to form the $3 \times 4$ matrix.
- **Coordinate System Flips**: Different datasets may use different coordinate conventions (e.g., OpenGL vs. DirectX).
- **Non-Orthogonal Result**: Method 1 (Arithmetic Mean) produces a non-orthogonal rotation matrix.
Estimates the radius and center of the scene to define the viewing frustum or sampling bounds.
Calculates the nearest point to all camera focal axes.
- **Time Complexity**: $O(N)$ for translation averaging. $O(N \cdot 3^3)$ for rotation averaging (matrix multiplication) plus $O(1)$ for SVD on a $3 \times 3$ matrix.
- **Memory Complexity**: $O(N)$ to store input poses. $O(1)$ auxiliary space.
- **Strengths**: Simple to implement (Method 1); robust to noise and outliers (Method 2 via SVD); provides a canonical reference frame.
- **Limitations**: Method 1 is not geometrically rigorous for rotations; Method 2 assumes all poses are equally weighted; sensitive to coordinate system inconsistencies across input poses.
- **When to Use**: Initializing NeRF training, setting up a central camera for visualization, or defining the bounding volume for ray sampling.
- **When Not to Use**: When poses are highly inconsistent or contain significant outliers (use robust statistics like RANSAC); when a specific target pose is required rather than an average.
Average pose calculation is a standard preprocessing step in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and 3D reconstruction pipelines.
